Letters “ H 8 “History Is Running Back- wards” is a provocative article. But I think David Brooks errs in framing traditionalism and modernity as an either/or, when in fact they exist in a both/and context. One can be both a traditionalist and a modern- ist simultaneously. The key, as Brooks notes, is that “a well- adjusted life consists of dar- ing explorations from a secure base.” Would that we all were so blessed to have that! Judy D. Cottrell Eugene, Ore. In dividing humanity into two neat psychological types— s tability-seeking tradition- alists and novelty-seeking progressives— Brooks misses an essential point: Psychology doesn’t exist in a vacuum; it constantly interacts with chang- ing social factors. People who not long ago may have readily switched jobs and moved cities are now more likely to stay in place because of the scarcity of new positions and lack of afford- able housing. Their psychology didn’t change—their circum- stances did. Our ancestors who ventured out of Africa 1.9 mil- lion years ago were likely seeking their next meal, not the thrill of adventure. These days, people are liable to deny science and seek safety in traditional institu- tions because the grandest cre- ation of modern technology— artificial intelligence—threatens everything about our way of life. Debates should focus not on psychological insecurity but on SEPTEMBER 2026 the technological, economic, and political decisions that are fostering material un certainty and pushing people to cling to a much safer past. Allen Frances, M.D. Carmel, Calif. The fact that the traditionalists whom Brooks discusses cannot even agree on when humani- ty’s “fall” occurred should raise doubts about their ideology. What they are constructing is less history than creation myth: As in the story of Adam and Eve, the fall occurs when people begin thinking for themselves. History and science teach us that there never was an Eden of perfect human harmony. Civi- lization was built painfully, and by most measurable standards,

C OM MONS life today is far better than it was in the past. The key to understanding the traditionalists is analyz- ing not the past they claim to describe but the present in which their appeals are gaining traction. Th eir movement has emerged as society has granted more rights to previously mar- ginalized groups. Beneath the traditionalists’ arguments lies a recurring sentiment: My group once had the authority to defi ne how society should function, and now it no longer does. If only people would stop questioning inherited traditions and defer once again to established authority, as defi ned by my group, then society could recover its lost harmony. Brooks suggests that cultivat- ing a sense of “rootedness” might help blunt the traditionalists’ appeal. But many Americans do not see themselves refl ected in what passes for American tradition. Our society does not make it easy for them to feel “rooted”—they do not see people like themselves in the lit- erature or history they study. We need to develop broader narra- tives that tell the country’s whole story. That in turn can culti- vate a broader sense of belong- ing. The humanities do need revival, as Brooks argues. But they should not be organized around a myth of decline. Th ey should be grounded instead in the founding principles that all people are created equal and possess inalienable rights. Th e continuing struggle to realize those ideals could provide the shared civic story in which all Americans might fi nd roots. Th omas M. Th urston Rosarito, Mexico Everything Is Free and Nothing Matters In the May issue, Noah Hawley described what he saw at Jeff Bezos’s Campfi re retreat. F. Scott Fitzgerald once wrote, “Let me tell you about the very rich. Th ey are diff erent from you and me.” Ernest Heming- way, in “The Snows of Kili- manjaro,” issued a reply, writ- ing, “Yes. They have more money.” I returned to their exchange while reading Noah Hawley’s essay about his time at Jeff Bezos’s retreat. Hawley demonstrates that Fitzgerald was indeed correct— and not merely in the way Hemingway considered. Bezos, Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, and their peers are so wealthy that they cannot spend all of their money in their lifetime. Th ey really are free from consequences. Neil Ravin Hampton, N.H. Billionaires are certainly hav- ing a moment—they’re more power ful than ever. But Noah Hawley’s assertion that they are living consequence-free lives is DISCUSSION & DEBATE false. After Elon Musk criticized Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill,” the president was clearly displeased, and a rift emerged between the two titans. But it was short-lived: Trump had the power to damage Musk’s busi- ness interests by canceling his lucrative contracts with the fed- eral government. Political lead- ers still have the power to rein in billionaires—if only they’re brave enough to try. Ken Taub Saint James, N.Y. I Found It: Th e Best Free Restaurant Bread in America In the May issue, Caity Weaver wrote a “fun article for people to read.” When I received my print edi- tion and saw that the cover story was about America’s “best free bread,” I was a little grumpy. Th e world is in chaos, democ- racy is withering, and this was the best Th e Atlantic could do? But because the story was on the cover, I sat down and read it. Turns out the answer was “Yes!” Caity Weaver’s article is an amazing novella. Her style is witty and brilliant, light and insightful. Th e article is a master- ful piece of journalism and a true delight to read, even with its wrenching moments. Th ank you for featuring something that pushed the chaos and gloom to the back of my mind for an hour. Stacey Wells Oakland, Calif. In the midst of a particularly taxing, soul-sucking, and bleak week, “I Found It: Th e Best Free Restaurant Bread in America” made me smile and laugh and remember that there are still lovely things to discover about the world. I’m very sorry for Weaver’s loss. I’m sure her par- ents would be proud that her articles have brought much joy to the world, and made a ran- dom computer programmer in Las Vegas not want to have a tantrum in the conference room. D I S PAT C H E S OPE NING A RGU M E N T THE BLUE BOOK IS BACK Th ank God. B Y WA LT H U N T E R A Ac ross the faded blue covers of the exam books in my attic, I can trace the arc of my academic career. I can still see the grades I r eceived on tests in “The Meaning of A bstraction in Modern Art” (A) and in N eur obiology (B–). Just the sight of the bo oklets is enough for me to feel the pres- s ur e to perform, to sculpt the contents of a semester ’s worth of knowledge into some fr esh shape. But by the time I became a college professor myself, in 2013, the blue bo ok had begun to disappear. Why strug- gle to discern student penmanship, or risk misplacing a final exam in the trunk of one ’s Subaru (to cite a completely hypo- thetical example), when tests, like every- thing else, can be administered on a laptop? Th e coronavirus made every aspect of education virtual, but even after it abated, 11

Dispatches in-person final exams remained out of favor for many classes. Part of the reason was simply administrative—the challenge of finding faculty or gradu- ate students to watch over the test-takers. But there was also a shift in how teachers appraised student learning. The blue book meant timed essays and hand written work, modes of assessment that felt regressive, cruel. It recalled an age of higher education—punitive and bleak, the domain of Dickens’s stern Mr. Gradgrind—that the mod- ern university was eager to out- grow. Not entirely, of course; some faculty still lugged boxes of blue books home in the snow and scribbled grades in red on the covers. But alternatives to the in-person exam proliferated: the capstone project, the take- home essay, the portfolio of selected work from the semester. The blue book seemed des- tined to become a relic, as obso- lete as cursive. But it had one virtue that hasn’t been easy to replicate: Cheating on a blue- book exam is difficult. When faculty moved away from in- person pen-and-paper exams, they assumed that cheating would be kept in check by honor codes, or by “locked” browsers, which would prevent students from accessing sites that would jog their memory or simply give them the answers. But these measures were never wholly effective. In a survey of under graduates published in 2020, 62 percent admitted to cheating in some manner. The advent of AI has only exacerbated the problem. In a matter of seconds, students can create an entire essay with the help of a chatbot. If they’re savvy, they can spend a bit more time to make it sound authen- tically human enough to evade detection by their professor. As 12 my colleague Rose Horowitch has reported, such cheating has become so prevalent that Princeton recently gave up on its venerable honor code. For 133 years, students had signed a pledge not to cheat, and pro- fessors had trusted them to do the right thing. In May, in the face of rampant AI-enabled cheating, the university’s fac- ulty voted to begin proctoring exams for the first time since the Gilded Age. Universities find them- selves in a surprising position. The only reliable way to evalu- ate what students have learned may be to bring back pen and paper. Faculty are reverting to in- person, handwritten assign- ments and timed essays— anything that keeps assessments offline. The unlikely hero of the day is the blue book, sales of which are up by as much as 80 percent for some universi- ties since 2023. Yet the blue book is more than a last redoubt against cheating. Despite its an tiquated appearance, the blue book encourages experimentation, even virtuosity. It deserves to live on not because of what it rejects but because of what it makes possible: thinking on the page, a hallmark of the humani- ties that is indispensable to their value—and essential to the kinds of human beings that a liberal-arts institution hopes to send out into the world. T h e b l u e b o o k hasn’t changed much for a hundred years or more, with its sky-blue tint and pale-red margin lines, its two neat staples and wide- open spacing, and its austere list of requirements on the cover (NAME, SUBJECT, CLASS, SECTION). The precise history of the blue book is lost to time. One origin story pinpoints its emergence in the 1920s at But- ler University; the pamphlet is said to have borrowed its distinctive hue from the uni- versity’s colors. Harvard lore suggests that the blue book is older still: By one account, a classics instructor, Evangeli- nus Apostolides Sophocles, burned a stack of blue-book exams to protest the universi- ty’s move from oral to written examinations in 1857. I realize that by advocating for the blue book in 2026, I might be engaging in the same opposition to progress as old Professor Sophocles. But to me, the blue book represents a time- less human activity—namely, trusting your mind to discover unknown capabilities. I think of my college-age self, looking up at the clock as I turned the page, crossed out a sentence, broke the tip of my pencil. I recall the satisfaction of filling one book and getting up from my desk to take another, the adrenaline of using my knowledge to improvise some- thing and then having more to say. What I learned by writing this way was distinct from what I learned by composing a five- paragraph essay, with its thesis statement, staid structure, and rote deployment of argument and evidence. Any AI agent can mimic that template. Taking a blue-book exam is an almost athletic endeavor, and not just because of the stamina it requires of both mind and hand. The test-taker is forced to compose an essay that will demonstrate their command of a semester’s or year’s worth of material. They have to summon the verve to tackle a prompt about the place of freedom in the Amer- ican novel, or the value of a human life in Hamlet, or what Whitman meant when he said SEPTEMBER 2026 that “the United States them- selves are essentially the great- est poem.” Staring down the empty pages of a blue book, I learned to throw myself into my writing. In the process, I discovered what I was capable of as a writer and a thinker. When you’ve done the read- ing and reviewed your lecture notes, you can feel like a bas- ketball player whose hours in the gym made possible a tran- scendent playoff performance, or like a musician whose end- less runs of arpeggios in a soundproof practice room allowed for a spectacular solo in the concert hall. Not every student can put pencil to paper for 90 minutes without looking up. Even the strongest students can struggle, at first, to answer the question, or to organize their thoughts. But this, too, is a reason to love the blue book. When stu- dents write, they write into un certainty. They court risk. No surrogate exists for feeling an idea form in your mind and trying to express that idea on the page. And wonderfully, for the instructor, the blue book documents how students strain their way to an answer or an argument. The marks on the page are indelible, and efforts to amend them leave marks of their own: furious erasing or hasty strike-throughs. The blue book is a record of first thoughts, instincts, intuitions. These fits and starts and failed experiments are a good thing—for the education of the individual and for the health of a society. The humanities are distinguished by the hab- its of mind that they inculcate, not for their success in forcing students to memorize facts. Among the most significant of these habits are a nimbleness of thought and a flexibility of

OPE NING A RGU M E N T argument, the ability to draw connections between diverse sets of facts. Those habits are honed by writing under pres- sure. Challenged by the blue book, students learn to iden- tify and stand behind their individual commitments. As their professor, I hope they carry that lesson beyond the classroom, beyond the uni- versity, and into the fractious world they enter as citizens. Often the key insight arrives just as time is expiring, and I love how no part of the book is out of bounds for a final thought at the buzzer. “Educa- tion is the single greatest thing Thoreau believes in,” one stu- dent sneaks into the margins of the final for my American- literature course. For the teacher, this is the pleasure of the blue book—despite its uni- form presentation and its rigid lineation, any part of it might reveal a sudden moonshot of an idea. Many of the best sentences appear on the back inside cover, such as this ending to an essay on Toni Morrison: “A good life is what we make it to be—now all we have to do is live it.” Students, of course, know what they’ve been taught: the timeline of the English Civil War, the structure of a sonnet by Gwendolyn Brooks, the development of a motif in a Mahler symphony. But the blue book demands more than a recitation of facts. It asks stu- dents to demonstrate not just that they know when or where something happened, but why it did. It asks them not just who wrote a poem, or when, but what the poem conveys about the world in which it was written. The best-prepared stu- dents, the ones who inhabit the history and poetry and music that have made up the semes- ter’s syllabus, find that they understand the material in ways they didn’t appreciate before they opened the blue book and the clock started ticking. Proponents of artificial intelligence have promised that, by removing certain ele- ments of the craft of writing, students can concentrate on making their work more pol- ished and their ideas more clearly defined. That’s a dan- gerous ruse. To see what a stu- dent has learned, look at the moment when they struggle to begin—and then tran- scend that struggle to create something genuinely surpris- ing. That’s the moment the full force of the writer’s mind takes possession of the process. When we eliminate the pos- sibility of writing badly or inco- herently, we eliminate writing’s greatest satisfaction: the feeling that we have stepped outside ourselves and are watching our own words fall together in the right order. What I describe sounds like a state of grace, but it’s also a furious act of intellec- tion and expression undertaken with only one’s study and wits to guide them. I’ve come to love handing out blue books on exam day and seeing the look of ready intelligence on my students’ faces. The essay they are about to write will be better than they think it can be. All they have to do is write it. Walt Hunter is a contributing editor at The Atlantic and an English professor at Case Western Reserve University. ILLUSTRATION BY BEN HICKEY 13

FIT N ESS Y O U C A L L T H AT A PULL-UP? The secretary of defense needs to work on his form. BY TOM BA RTLETT ete Hegseth wants us to watch him sweat. Videos of the secretary of defense in a T-shirt and shorts working out alongside military person- nel have become a trademark of his tenure. He has been filmed running on Omaha Beach, swinging a kettle bell on a university campus, and doing jumping jacks on an amphibious assault ship. In one clip, Heg seth pumps iron with troops at the Guantánamo Bay naval base— or, as a Defense Department X account put it, “America’s @SECWAR CRUSHED 44 reps on the bench after a morning run.” But did he really crush those reps? Each time a new episode of Boot Camp Pete drops, crit- ics skewer his form and mock his endurance. They insist that he’s all flex and no fundamen- tals. In that bench-press clip, for example, he doesn’t fully extend his arms, making the exercise far easier and inflating his total. A few seconds into the clip, you can hear someone P 14 yell, “All the way down, all the way up!” Hegseth fails to heed that helpful cue. Such nitpicking would be uncharitable if Hegseth were just another 40-something dad getting a lift in at Planet Fit- ness. But these are highlight reels, posted by the Pentagon. Plus, the former Fox News host isn’t exactly known for withholding judgment him- self: Recall how, last Septem- ber, he gathered the nation’s generals and admirals together so that he could upbraid them for being overweight. He told them that leaders set the stan- dard and that when “you let the small stuff go, the big stuff eventually goes.” With Hegseth’s wisdom in mind, let’s examine what the United States military’s train- ing manuals have to say about proper exercise form. Short answer: a lot. You’ll find hun- dreds of pages spelling out precisely how to perform all manner of movements, includ- ing how to stretch your thighs (“grasp the left ankle and pull toward the left buttock”), how to plank (“forearms flat on the ground, forming a triangle”), and how to throw a four-pound ball from a seated position (“do not throw the medicine ball like shooting a basketball”). These manuals are replete with charts, bullet points, and illustrations. The Army’s Holistic Health and Fitness Testing manual provides detailed instructions, accom- panied by photographs, on the bench press, warning that you must not “jerk or shrug the shoulders, arch the back, or allow the hips to rise off the bench” (note to Secretary Heg- seth: p. 65, Appendix B). Standards vary across branches, even for basic exer- cises. Take the push-up. For the Army’s fitness test, soldiers must do what’s known as a hand-release push-up, requir- ing them to stick their arms straight out to the side after each repetition. The Marine guide devotes several hundred words to describing how to do a tradi- tional push-up, specifying that soldiers “may not rest their chest on the deck except as required to ensure that the upper arms are at least parallel to the deck.” In the Air Force, your feet cannot be more than 12 inches apart, and you must maintain a “rigid head to heel form.” These are direc- tives rather than suggestions. Failure to meet the standard results in a “no-go,” in military parlance, meaning you haven’t passed that portion of the test. Hegseth’s push-ups wouldn’t pass muster in any branch. Last summer, Hegseth and Health Secretary Robert F. Ken- nedy Jr. kicked off the “Pete & Bobby Challenge,” in which participants attempt to do 50 pull-ups and 100 push-ups in less than 10 minutes. Heg- seth’s push-ups are more like half-ups: In the ones captured on video, he doesn’t go through SEPTEMBER 2026 the full range of motion. His substandard technique is ironic because he’s on record ridicul- ing others for their lack of push-up prowess. In his 2024 book, The War on Warriors, Hegseth mocks women soldiers who can do only “ten push-ups at a pop” and refers to a trans- gender woman as a “ten-push- up kind of guy.” To be fair, Hegseth’s pull- up form, at times, is more or less textbook. The issue is con- sistency: Hegseth can’t seem to maintain the standard for the duration of the competi- tion, and raises his knees to his chest to give himself additional oomph. This is known as “kip- ping” and is forbidden in an eight-page pull-up guide pub- lished by the Marines. In one clip, Hegseth kips while using an underhand grip, which tech- nically makes what he’s doing a chin-up—an exercise often considered less challenging than a pull-up. (The Marine guide permits both, though kipping is always forbidden.) Accord- ing to the guide: “Poor quality work will prevent you from get- ting the most from your work- out and can lead to injury.” Hegseth’s work is, by Marine standards, poor. Hegseth claims at the end of the video that he finished in less than six minutes, which would be impressive if he weren’t flouting the rules and sacri- ficing form for speed. What’s more, he’s doing these exercises incorrectly during a challenge that bears his name. Given all of this, it’s impossible to have confidence in the validity of Hegseth’s self-reported feat. Granted, I am not a trained grader of military exercises. Prior to perusing these manu- als, I wasn’t aware that your arms need to be at a 45-degree angle in relation to your trunk

Dispatches for the modified bent-leg body twist, or that it is impera- tive to point your toes to the rear for the prone row. I was entirely unfamiliar with the squat bender and the quadra- plex. Nor did I know, before watching an Army instructional video, how to swing a kettlebell. As it happens, neither does Hegseth, who, in January, was filmed swinging a kettlebell with recruits at UCLA. You’re supposed to keep the kettlebell near your body and generate momentum with your legs and hips. Instead, Hegseth squats, as if doing deep knee bends, and brings the weight far too close to the ground, putting strain on his shoulders and back. This is wrong, according approach and abilities. But he said he stresses to his students the importance of going all the way up and all the way down, whether it’s a pull-up, push-up, or bench press. I also asked Maureen Le Boeuf what she made of the “Pete & Bobby Chal- lenge” video. Le Boeuf is a retired brigadier general and the first and only woman to head the physical- education department at West Point, a position known as “master of the sword.” She said that noth- ing she saw from the defense secretary in that video would have counted if she had been the grader, and she has graded thousands of such tests. “His pull-ups or chin-ups and the kicking that he does— you would never allow that. You’d stop somebody; you’d say, ‘Okay, you’re done,’ ” Le Boeuf said. “He just keeps kicking, and it’s not a good look.” She allowed that he might have been exhausted in those clips, but the Army doesn’t usually recognize fatigue as an excuse. And it’s hard to forgive such lapses and corner-cutting from someone who, as Le Boeuf put it, is “real big on standards.” In response to an inquiry about the criticism of Heg- seth’s workouts, Joel Valdez, the acting Pentagon press secretary, insisted that Heg- seth was being unfairly sin- gled out. “Have you ever seen Lloyd Austin’s form? Did the Atlantic ever ask about it?” he wrote. “The answer to both of those questions is no.” That’s true, but Austin, the previ- ous secretary of defense, was not known for posting self- promotional exercise content on social media. He did, how- ever, complete Ranger School and Airborne School, com- mand the 10th Mountain Division in Afghanistan, lead the fight against the Islamic State, and earn a Silver Star. Bottom: Secretary Hegseth’s form is inconsistent. In one clip from the “Pete & Bobby Challenge,” he does a chin-up and raises his knees to give himself additional oomph—a technique known as “kipping” that is forbidden by the Marines. to Joel Del Rosario, a retired Marine and a kettlebell coach. Del Rosario told me he’s glad to see Hegseth encouraging better fitness in the military, and he noted that, in his experience, pretty much everyone who gives the kettlebell a whirl fails at first. He said he’d be honored if asked to show Hegseth how to do the exercise properly. I consulted other military exercise experts too. Among them was Stew Smith, a former Navy SEAL and the author of a series of books about prep- ping to qualify for the Special Forces, including one on the Ranger Physical Assessment. A former Army National Guard infantry officer, Hegseth has bemoaned slipping standards across the military, including at the Ranger School— even though he never completed the famously grueling 61-day lead- ership and fitness course. Kevin Dowdell’s Boys COURTESY OF THE DOWDELL FAMILY When a veteran firefighter vanished on 9/11, his teenage sons went looking for him. By Sally Jenkins Photographs by Haruka Sakaguchi 17

o a firefighter who is inside one, a fire cre- ates as much dark- ness as heat. Flames start bright but throw off smoke that can swathe every- thing in pitch black. Lieutenant Kevin Dowdell did not fight fires so much as he groped through and problem- solved them, relying on half-blind judgment and expertise— and his fellow firefighters to keep flaming debris off his back. At the cindering end of a successful 24- hour shift with the New York City Fire Department, Kevin would hang up his helmet, so ash-rubbed that it looked salty, and drive home to his wife and two sons in Rockaway Beach, Queens. “Oh, we had a good job last night,” he’d say, elated as well as exhausted. By “good,” his family knew, he meant the fire had been big. In his innermost firefighter’s heart, Kevin liked it when the alarms went off. A good job broke the tedium of drills and doughnut- dunking in the firehouse kitchen. It called on Kevin’s whole mind and body; he had to calculate burn rates and airflow while wielding 40 pounds of gear. Fire needs four elements: oxy- gen, heat, fuel, and a chemical reaction. Deprive a fire of even one of those, and it goes out. But in New York— a steel-stacked, deep- tunneled metropolis with architecture ranging from tenements to glass towers— the interaction of the elements is complex. My wife and I drove by that unlit sign on the hot May afternoon when we moved from New York to the interior of Maine. It was 2020. The 100,000th American was about to die of COVID. And I was starting my dream job. Arriving at Bates College, we passed the empty quad, took a left, and pulled our U-Haul up to our new home: a century-old colonial just off campus, ringed by a tangle of blooming lilacs and wild blackberries. As we began unpacking, alternating between unloading boxes and marveling at the house—twice the size and half the rent of our Queens apartment— an older man crossed the street and intro- duced himself as a retired faculty member. We made Norman Rockwell small talk. His wife, crouched in a shaded corner of her garden, waved with a pair of pruning shears. The setting was impossibly idyllic. And it was not the first time in my academic career that I’d had occasion to reflect on my good fortune. My path to the professoriat had been a fairy tale. In 2014, I went straight from my bachelor’s degree at Haverford to a fully funded Ph.D. program in comparative literature at NYU. I got the email on December 23, 2019, a Christmas miracle. As I got to know Ava, I was surprised to discover that she viewed central Maine as a Stephen King–esque hell, a place where ancient prejudices and violence lay just beneath the friendly college- town facade. She regaled my wife and me with stories of alleged racial offenses, both major and minor, and generally made it clear that she thought Lewiston— an island of diversity in an otherwise famously homogenous, if not notably reaction- ary, state— was a hub of white supremacy. One evening, Ava confessed to me that when she drove through town and spied the local “crackers” sitting on their porches (not unlike the very porch we were sitting on), she sometimes thought to herself that these townies would probably like to kill her. I didn’t know what to make of Ava’s views. I won’t pretend that my sensibilities were inflamed by the word cracker, but the epithet also didn’t seem like one that a college administrator should be using—especially at a school that admits a not-insignificant num- ber of white, working-class Mainers. I also had a difficult time taking seriously the idea that I had moved to a place with would- be Klansmen around every corner. I grew up outside Harris burg, Pennsylvania—another deindustrialized, permanently revitalizing urban center—and Lewiston felt familiar to me. The people I met were nice, hardworking; they minded their own business. I don’t think it ever occurred to Ava that I could have come from a similar place and similar people. But although I sometimes found the things she said classist and even offensive, I also genuinely liked Ava. She had a fast wit and a quick laugh. I left freshly baked sourdough baguettes on her porch; we commiserated during power outages. Ava struck me as per- haps a touch paranoid, but she was also obviously smart. More important, she was a well-credentialed authority on racism, and I took such people seriously. Why wouldn’t I? I’d never had great enthusiasm for identity politics; I’d been a socialist since my early 20s, and it had generally been my expe- rience that liberals were as eager to talk about race as they were uneager to talk about class. Yet I also assumed that conservative complaints about “wokeness,” a term just coming into vogue as a pejorative, were essentially Fox News hysteria. At Haverford, the campus politics were of the earthy, stoner, peacenik variety—more focused on “late capitalism” and Presi- dent Obama’s drone warfare than flamboyant identitarianism. The path to becoming a tenure-track professor can be grueling—the system asks people to spend the prime of their life moving from low-paying job to low-paying job, from one state to another to another, all in the hopes of one day getting a permanent position. Because many universities cap the number of courses that adjuncts can teach (to avoid having to comply with federal health-care mandates), many of them have to teach half a dozen or more per semester spread across different local colleges— a practice known as “freeway flying”—to cobble together a living. One in four non-tenure-track college educators relies on public assistance. One in three earns less than $25,000 a year. Mia’s position at Bates was about to expire, and so I assumed that we would take the rare opportunity to hire her onto the tenure track. Once again, I watched a committee talk itself out of an obvious choice. On a cold morning a few days into 2025, the group arrived at its final decision: We would not be hiring Mia, a result that made it likely that this would be her last semester at Bates, and perhaps her last semester as an academic. If Mia had been a mediocre teacher or scholar, that would be one thing. But the committee agreed that she was absolutely qualified. There just happened to be another “diverse” candidate who was judged to 79

be a marginally better fit, and who did more to expand our cur- ricular offerings. I had watched the college chew up and spit out enough non-tenure-track professors that Mia’s fate shouldn’t have come as a surprise, but it did. I saw clearly now what should have been obvious all along. Bates was not a good place to work, nor a moral one. And the problem went beyond a single college: Bates was a node in a higher-education system that offered teenagers an uncertain future in exchange for often unpayable debt, and that asked scholars— enticed by the tweedy dream of a kind of faculty life that has long since been clubbed to death—to keep waiting for the real job that would surely come after the temporary job, and the next temporary job, and the next. I had been spared all that. And I was on the cusp of getting the very thing I had wanted since I was a 21-year-old English major in my modernism professor’s wood-lined office, declaring that I would like to do her job one day. My senior colleagues in environmental studies talked about my tenure as if it were a foregone conclusion and openly discussed how I was next in line for program chair. The same January morning we decided not to hire Mia, Bates’s president announced that I was one of four professors—and the only non-tenured faculty member—whom my colleagues had voted onto the powerful Strategic Planning Steering Committee, a body composed of the president himself, various vice presidents, and a member of the board of trustees. I was on the inside track of an inside track, but it felt hollow. Sitting in that last search-committee meeting, deliberating the fate of a person who, like me, had spent years chasing after a career that felt more like a calling, I was unexpectedly gripped by a granite certainty. I did not want to keep doing this. My aca- demic Stockholm syndrome—You do not leave the tenure track— subsided in a rush. Five years after my adviser had likened me to the last dinosaur, I decided to walk my academic career into a tar pit rather than wait for the asteroid. I sat in my car after the deliberation about Mia ended and sent an email to a confidant explaining that I intended to leave Bates. T h e s t o r y o f elite higher education’s hiring and labor prac- tices and the story of its decades-long creep toward progressive extremism are not separate or even contradictory. They are the same story. In 1969, a survey of 60,000 professors found that 27 percent identified as moderate, 28 percent as conservative, and 46 percent as liberal or left. Now, at some of this country’s top universities, only single-digit percentages of faculty identify as conservative. A 2025 survey of Harvard faculty placed that number at 9 percent. How this happened is no mystery: The very system that was designed to protect the faculty’s right to free thought collapsed. By 1980, as many as two-thirds of American college professors were tenured. Today, only about a quarter are. We went from a world where most faculty members could say what they think without fear of being fired to one where most people teaching college courses have to worry that their contract won’t be renewed if they cause intellectual offense. It is not surprising that a profes- soriat disproportionately composed of contract workers would also be one that could be pressured into groupthink. 80 In a consultant-led meeting I attended near the end of my time at the college, one month into Donald Trump’s second term, the small group of professors and senior administrators present was asked to share what it saw as Bates’s greatest strengths and weaknesses. One of my colleagues said that the college’s greatest strength was its commitment to DEI. Another said that the col- lege’s greatest weakness was that it could be even more committed to DEI. Someone lamented that our ties to the Wabanaki Nations could have been stronger. As snow turned into slush, I walked by a flyer pasted to a campus building announcing the college’s annual sex week. The technicolor poster proclaimed that Bates would be hosting a game of “dildo ring toss” and would provide “exploration tables” replete with sex toys. Once, I might have seen in that poster a symptom of everything wrong with the college—money wasted on weird bullshit, organized by bureaucrats whose jobs nobody could explain. Now I found it all oddly refreshing. What was Bates if not a place devoted to risk-free ideological masturbation? For a week, at least, we could be honest about it. Months later, I joined The Atlantic as a full-time staff writer. I was busy enjoying my first fall free from academia when I heard the news: At the November faculty meeting, Bates professors would vote on whether to suspend the Race, Power, Privilege, and Colo- nialism requirement, which was set to begin in 2026. Cooler minds at the college had evidently judged that, given the political climate, now was not exactly the best time for mandatory courses on the physics of white supremacy or the chemistry of colonialism; such a nakedly politicized curriculum, in fact, could make Bates a target of the current administration. The new legislation proposed that implementation of the requirement be paused until 2029—not coincidentally, after the next presidential election. I thought I’d feel vindicated. I had argued all along that the RPPC was pointless, unworkable, mad. Now it was dead. Yet, unexpectedly, I was disappointed. Here was one last sign that it had all meant nothing. I recalled the dean’s faint embarrassment, years earlier, when I’d said that I was proud to join a school with an abolitionist past. Although the dead cannot speak, I must assume that embarrassment runs both ways. Bates was founded in 1855 on the principle that a man is a man wherever he is found and whatever color his skin. In the decade that followed, the college furnished from its ranks 173 students willing to spill their blood for the cause of the Union and human liberation. One of these abolitionist-educated men was Holman S. Melcher, who left Bates to join the 20th Maine Regiment. A year later, at Gettysburg, he helped lead the bayonet charge down the hill at Little Round Top and into the maw of an advancing Confederate force. Now this same college could not find the spine required to simply stand by a curricular change that its faculty and adminis- trators had breathlessly, earnestly, performatively insisted was an imperative because it was nothing less than a matter of justice. The vote was unanimous. Tyler Austin Harper is a staff writer at The Atlantic. SEPTEMBER 2026

By Scott Stossel To announce that you are embarking on a course of psycho analytic training today is tantamount, in many quarters, to admitting that you plan to treat your patients using astrology or by parsing the entrails of a goat. To say that you are undergoing psycho analysis as a patient is to reveal that you are entrusting your mental health to a witch doctor. So if I were to tell you that a respected neuroscientist has undertaken to exhume Sigmund Freud and make a case for both his theory of mind and his psycho analytic method as the best—indeed, the only—approach that can cure emotional disorders, you would likely rate that a quixotic project, and its author perhaps a candidate for serious therapy himself. Freud’s cultural and scientific influence crested some 70 years ago, and much of psychiatry’s history since then has consisted of a renunciation of the man, his concepts, and his therapeutic techniques so com- prehensive as to have an edge of savagery, even ven- geance, to it. He has been deemed a sexist, a misogy- nist, a bully, a narcissist, a homophobe, a pervert, an addict, an opportunist, a plagiarist, a fabulist, and a scientific fraud, as well as a disloyal friend and a credit- stealing protégé. Not to mention a bungling, incompe- tent therapist— “a dogmatist who browbeat his patients and consistently failed to mark the crucial difference between their fantasies and his own.” (So sums up the flap copy on a collection of Freud-filleting essays by 18 psychiatrists, philosophers, historians, and others compiled in 1998 by Frederick Crews, a literary critic and onetime devout Freudian turned virulent heretic.) If coroners were to pin an actual time of death on Freudianism, they might specify 1963. That year, the philosopher of science Karl Popper held up psycho- analytic theory as the archetypal instance of what he called “pseudo science”: Worse than mere bad science, psycho analysis was, in being untestable, simply not SEPTEMBER 2026 tion of Freud? And why? To take the second question first, here’s one reason: What has followed Freud- ianism has not been, by many reckonings, any bet- ter. In the 1970s, the mental-health profession fled from such squishy psychological concepts as transfer- ence and countertransference, the death drive, and seduction theory— as well as more outlandish ones like penis envy, castration anxiety, and the Oedipal complex— and leaned instead into “biological psy- chiatry,” which had emerged from the drug discover- ies of the 1950s and ’60s. Physiological notions took hold, such as the “cat- echolamine hypothesis of affective disorders,” which attributed anxiety and depression to deficits of the neurotransmitters norepinephrine and dopamine. Three decades later, in the 1990s, the “chemical- imbalance theory of depression” arrived, tying depres- sion and other mood disorders to dysregulation of another neuro transmitter, serotonin. Psycho analysts’ highly subjective assessments gave way to the osten- sibly more objective measurements provided by neuroscientific instruments that can capture brain activity, such as EEGs, PET scans, and fMRIs. Doc- tors turned to genetic testing to help identify various temperament types and emotional predispositions, and relied on standardized questionnaires assessed for their validity in diagnosing mental illness. In repudiating Freudianism and touting the field’s proper medical grounding, science-based psychiatry confidently predicted that measurable success was soon to come. That’s not what happened. Biologi- cal psychiatry “overreached, overpromised, over- diagnosed, overmedicated,” as the Harvard medical historian Anne Harrington put it in 2019. Which raises the question of whether psychiatry has simply exchanged one form of witchcraft for another. The champions of so-called anti-psychiatry and critical psychiatry—now emboldened by Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and the MAHA movement— certainly think so. So do some leading figures in biological psychiatry. As the head of the National Institute of Mental Health from 2002 to 2015, Thomas Insel tried to root America’s approach to mental-health care more firmly in brain physiology and the emerging understanding of genetics than in the nebulous concepts of Freudianism. But in 2017, when he looked back on the $20 billion he’d spent on 85

Freud goes on to note that some of the most accomplished figures in history— Plato, Michelangelo, Leonardo da Vinci— were gay, and ends by saying that although psychoanalysis can help her son become happier, less neurotic, and more productive, none of that will have anything to do with his sexual orientation. I suspect more than a few Freud detractors will be surprised to read this. By Solms’s own estimation, there might be “nobody alive who has spent more time with Freud than I have.” But Solms is no doctrinaire acolyte, as guardians of the Freudian flame have tended to be. Ernest Jones, an influential early director of the Inter- national Psychoanalytical Association, believed his role was to create a secret committee “like the Paladins of Charlemagne” to protect Freudian theory against heresy. Solms, in contrast, embraces some major criti- cisms of Freud, calling the death drive, for example, “an egregious error.” As for Freud’s rather “idiosyn- cratic” theories about sex, Solms writes, “I don’t think there’s any getting around the conclusion that Freud had this stuff seriously muddled.” Part of Solms’s premise in this book is implicit and inarguable: Despite the attempts to purge Freudian- ism from psychiatry, its tropes, terms, and concepts— the unconscious; the id, ego, and superego; sublima- tion; defense mechanisms; the obsession with sex; the importance of early-childhood experiences— have seeped so deeply into our cultural limbic system that they live on in the shared metaphors and terminology we use to discuss personality and mental health: Frank is “anal”; Mary is “repressed”; Donald Trump is a “nar- cissist” and an “egomaniac”; Jill Biden was “in denial.” When Freud died, in 1939, W. H. The first is that Freud deserves credit for neuroscientific prescience. A recent history of neuroscience states baldly that “Freud had nothing novel or insightful to say about how the brain worked.” On the contrary, according to Solms: Many prevailing theories about how the brain func- tions were first worked out by Freud. For instance, Solms writes, Freud effectively identified the way that short-term memories get consolidated into long-term

(To bolster his case here, Solms marshals the very man who identified that particular mechanism, Eric Kandel, who won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for doing so, and who agrees with Solms that psycho analysis is “the most coherent and intel- lectually satisfying view of the mind” we have, and that neuroscience is the “new intellectual framework” that can reinvigorate psychiatry.) Or consider Freudianism’s key concept, the un conscious. Freud argued that our personalities and behaviors are governed by a maelstrom of hidden drives and motivations mostly unknown to our con- scious selves. What we experience as our “conscious life” is in fact only a post hoc rationalization of things we are doing for other reasons, a devastating blow against not just human rationality but even free will. For years, evidence of the unconscious seemed inaccessible to objective science. How can you prove the existence of something that none of us, by defini- tion, can be subjectively aware of ? But technologies unavailable to Freud have demonstrated that much of what happens in the brain is in fact unconscious. Studies using fMRI machines have revealed that when frightening images or angry faces are shown to peo- ple too fast for them to consciously perceive them, their brains nevertheless register the fear stimuli: The machines detect a flare of activity in the amygdala, which is followed by a surge in heart rate, blood pres- sure, and stress hormones, among other responses. The feeling of fear in the body then breaks into con- sciousness, and the brain makes decisions in response to that. It has become hard to deny that, at least in basic outline, Freud was right about the unconscious. S o l m s’s s e c o n d explicit claim is, if anything, even more provocative. There is abundant evidence, he writes, that psychoanalysis and its offshoots “are astoundingly effective”—in some cases, he argues, “as dependable as, say, insulin is at managing type 1 diabetes, or as the HPV vaccine is at preventing cer- vical cancer. In sup- port, Solms cites a number of studies and papers from the past 40 years to show that psychoanalytic- style talk therapy is more effective than anti- depressants or electro convulsive therapy for depres- sion, or than anti psychotics for schizophrenia. He also cites research demonstrating that psychoanalysis has a robust “sleeper effect”— that is, symptoms con- tinue to improve long after the treatment has ended. Technologies unavailable to Freud have demonstrated that much of what happens in the brain is in fact unconscious. These results are so striking that I decided to look at the underlying studies, and some other relevant ones. I found that Solms is highly selective in what he cites, and elides a lot of nuance (and sometimes directly contradictory evidence) in service of his case for psychoanalytic-style therapy and against other forms of therapy, especially pharmacotherapy. Cherry-picking is not unusual (especially when deal- ing with studies that are hard to compare), but the conclusions that flow from it are usually accompanied by a degree of circumspection. Solms’s verdicts are categorically blunt: “Nearly every psychiatric disorder listed and defined in the standard diagnostic manuals is best understood and treated, not pharmacologically, but psychologically.” And: “There are, as things stand, no physiological cures in psychiatry.” And perhaps most bracing: “The main- stay of modern psychiatry— psychopharmacology— is for the most part a defence against facing the facts about what our patients really need. It is a way of suppressing symptoms instead of asking what they mean and fixing that.” Solms’s position aligns him, probably unintention- ally, with the public pronouncements that RFK Jr. has issued about SSRI anti depressants in his role as HHS secretary, which made the American Psychiatric Asso- ciation convention in May jangly with tension. Anti- depressants are useless, Kennedy has said at various times; they are more addictive than heroin, result in “brain damage,” and could be partly responsible for school shootings. None of this is true. But one reason demagoguing against medication has been easy is that the biological model of psychiatry— although filling the coffers of pharmaceutical companies— has delivered no panaceas, instead fueling cycles of disenchanted over- reaction. (Today, one in six Americans takes an anti- depressant; no wonder APA attendees were on edge.) Solms does concede that while no physiological cures exist in psychiatry, physiological treatments can remediate symptoms. That Advil doesn’t “cure” pain doesn’t stop people from taking the drug to alleviate it. Still, his broadside against pharmacology seems overbroad: Although it is surely true that many of those who take SSRI anti depressants do not need, and should not be on, them, it is also true that many oth- ers would be debilitated, if not dead, without them. Before Freud became a psychiatrist, he himself was a neuroanatomist. Some of his early research was on the gonads of eels and the nervous systems of crayfish. But given the tools available to him in the 1890s, he kept bumping up against the limits of what the physi- cal brain could reveal about the functioning of the mind. Frustrated and in need of money, he put aside the microscope, opened a private practice, and began focusing instead on clinical observation of patients, and 87

He sometimes expressed embarrassment at this approach. “It still strikes me myself as strange that the case histo- ries I write should read like short stories and that, as one might say, they lack the serious stamp of science,” he reflected in his foundational Studies on Hysteria in 1895. In his sec- ond paragraph, Solms ushers in a depressed physician named Teddy P, who gets dumped by his girlfriend after struggling with both premature ejaculation and erectile dysfunction (perhaps a bit on the nose for a book about Sigmund Freud). When Teddy’s case becomes acute— in addition to depression and sexual dysfunction, he develops insom- nia, headaches, brain fog, seizures, and evidence of pos- sible dementia— Solms takes him on as a patient. He determines that Teddy’s underlying disease is psycho- logical, not neurological (the seizures had made that an open question), and attributes much of what ails Teddy to the cascading effects of drugs and treatments he’s being given for his depression, anxiety, insomnia, and pain. Solms weans him off his medications and embarks with him on a course of psychoanalysis. Then he puts Teddy aside, leaving the reader in suspense for 258 pages before resuming the account of his fate. 88 For all his extensive neuromedical training, Solms makes a point of describing the work of psycho- analysis as “less like science and more like a practical trade. Long experience leads to familiarity with many different kinds of glitch and suggests many different kinds of fix.” Some people— and by some people, I might mean me— derive a certain solace from under- standing their anxiety and depression as, in effect, mechanical failures, not moral ones: a snag in the temperamental wiring here, an unfortunate genetic variant there, a dys regulation of neurotransmitters not unlike the problems with insulin regulation in a diabetic’s pancreas. But Solms’s contention, drawing from Freud, is that those mechanical problems can be fixed only as part of a wholesale realignment of unconscious drives and emotional needs. That worked for Solms: He had been plagued by a severe death anxiety since he was a little boy, when his older brother suffered brain damage in a freak accident, but was cured by a course of analysis on the couch of Clifford Yorke, a British World War II veteran who had helped care for survivors after the liberation of Bergen-Belsen. Teddy recovers. (This is no spoiler; readers could hardly have been expecting otherwise.) After four years of arduous work with Solms, revisiting early-childhood experiences and his relationship with his mother, his depression and anxiety lift, his sexual and romantic- attachment issues abate, his growing conscious aware- ness frees him from damaging unconscious compul- sions. He becomes an outstanding doctor. The treatment involves all kinds of unexpected twists and turns, and Solms deploys a lot of Freudian tools— dream analysis, free association, breaking down defense mechanisms, recovering buried memories, transference and counter transference, and elaborate (too elaborate, if you ask me) feats of interpretation by the analyst. To someone with my firmly materialist leanings, it all seems a bit much. But I was struck by two things Solms writes in dif- ferent places earlier in the book. One is that the aim of psychotherapy, at its core, is simply “to help our patients find better ways of meeting their emotional needs.” Whatever you think of the whole complicated Freudian edifice, who could take issue with that? The other is: “Psychoanalysis is a cure wrought by loving your neighbor as yourself.” Solms has set out to com- plete the Freudian project by giving it a neuroscientific basis—but maybe the more important accomplish- ment is to have restored to psychiatry its humanity. Jim’s strongest connections were with his buddies at the bar. On sum- mer breaks from college, Russo returned to Gloversville, in upstate New York, and his dad would get him on the road crew. When work ended, they would head home, hit- ting pubs along the way. At each stop, Jim would regale the regulars with a story about something that had happened on the job that day. “He would pay attention to what worked in Roadhouse A,” Russo said in 2025, “so that when he got to Roadhouse B, he would remember what got a laugh and what didn’t, and so he would change the story.” Jim would tell the same story over many days, cutting and shaping, finding the beats. “There’s a word for that,” Russo said. “It’s called revision.” Revision, a refined term that Jim would never have used, is a staple of M.F.A. programs, such as the one his son attended at the University of Arizona. When Russo graduated in 1980, the experimental fiction of William Gass and Kurt Von- negut was in vogue, but he much preferred the shambling shaggy- dog novels of Twain and Dickens, whose humor arose not from for- mal innovation but from the foibles of flawed characters (like his dad), many of them poor and unlettered (ditto). Early on, Russo threw in his lot with Tom and Huck and Jim, with David Copperfield and Oliver Twist— characters whose humble beginnings offer a vantage from which to see the absurdity of an unjust world. Beginning with the 1986 pub- lication of his first novel, Mohawk, Russo has filled 10 novels, plus many essays and short stories, 89

Culture & Critics with portraits of men born with few gifts save their wits, making their way in an economy not set up to reward their kind. The bulk of his fiction is set in New York, in towns like Gloversville, where the good jobs have vanished (the glove-making trade there— once responsible for 90 percent of gloves sold in America— was by the 1950s already being replaced by imports). In these places, it’s unclear who is slinging more bull, the semi- employed men in bars or the educated civic “leaders,” such as mayors and bankers, promising that good times will return. In Russo’s best work, especially his classic trilogy, set in fictional North Bath— Nobody’s Fool (1993), Everybody’s Fool (2016), and Somebody’s Fool (2023)— his characters’ banter, crude and self-knowing, reminds us that the worst effects of the modern economy are present not in the landscape but in the soulscape, the fractured lives and identities of obsolete workers. Their barroom bravado is a front, masking inner hurt, or just bewilderment. In the novelist’s business of exploring what’s inside people’s heads— the way we all think more than we can say— Russo is the peer of Jonathan Franzen and Meg Wolitzer, even if his characters think in fewer syllables. At 77, Russo has published a new novel, Under the Falls, that at first seems to be a break with his past work. The characters are young, mostly in their mid-30s, and the protagonist, Tyler Sinclair, is honest- to-goodness rich. After high school, he left Stone Mountain, another of Russo’s fictional upstate hamlets, riding his guitar to stardom. When he blew out of town, he left behind a toxic love triangle and a paralyzed buddy, the victim of a near drowning that many blamed Tyler for. In the years since, he has milked the town, and a Mellencamp-like image as a boy from the sticks, for songwriting material. Now Tyler has come back to a place he never wanted to see again. Stone Mountain’s denizens feel the same way about him. At his much-ballyhooed return show, he and his band are pelted with eggs. On the way out of town, the band’s limousine is mysteriously driven off the road, and during his convalescence in Stone Mountain, Tyler gets caught up in local intrigue involving dope dealing, manslaughter, and police corruption. Under the Falls is a short potboiling book, lacking the finer-grained mind reading and social texture that Russo excels at (the acknowledgments note that it began as a TV-pilot script). Yet in the Russo tra- dition, it’s about a boy whose hometown has mired him in grief but also given him the stories that will lift him out of it. And tucked into its harebrained (if thoroughly enjoyable) plotting is a line that could well be Russo’s artistic credo. Tyler is relieved, and a bit amazed, to see how Doc, his paralyzed friend, has 90 made a decent life for himself, with his own trailer, wheelchair, and car (a hearse tricked out with hand controls), funded by his “vast criminal enterprise.” “As an artist,” Russo writes, “Tyler has more than once wondered whether, under the right circum- stances, or maybe the wrong ones, simply living life might qualify as art, and it occurs to him that his duty here is simple: to surrender his reservations and simply admire the man.” A m o n g a l l the hard-luck men in these hard- UNDER T H E FA L L S Richard Russo KNOPF SEPTEMBER 2026 scrabble towns, the ones who compound their bad luck with bad choices interest Russo the most. His emblematic figure is Donald “Sully” Sullivan, the star of the North Bath trilogy, a saga about one man surfing the arc of the 20th century that invites com- parison to Richard Ford’s Frank Bascombe books and John Updike’s Rabbit quartet, also anchored by troubled male protagonists. But Sully, whom we first meet in late middle age as a handyman with a bum knee— flashbacks fill in his tortured boyhood, his high-school-football career, his World War II service, his failed marriage— is on the opposite side of the class divide from those men. Bascombe is a writer, then a real-estate agent, and Harry “Rabbit” Ang- strom dies rich, fat on sales from the car dealership he inherited from his father-in-law. Sully never has a penny extra until his old age, when he has some luck with the ponies and then inherits his landlady’s decaying house— and discovers how disconcerted he is by the taste of middle-class life. “He’d always sus- pected that life’s deck was stacked in favor of those with means,” Russo writes. Now what? For Rabbit and Bascombe, the American dream is real, or real enough. For Sully, the idea that he was “now and forevermore insulated against adversity” just doesn’t compute; it feels like a cruel joke. And for Russo, the place that Sully inhabits is at least as interesting as the man himself—a signature of his fiction, which specializes in ensemble nov- els. “One of the good things about small towns,” Russo writes in his Pulitzer Prize winner, Empire Falls (2001), set in a postindustrial Maine hamlet, “was that they accommodated just about everyone; the lame and disfigured were all your neighbors, and seeing them every day meant that after a while you stopped noticing what made them different.” The important thing is how they’re alike on the inside. In his sad-sack locales, characters face their predicaments with a mix of resilience, disappoint- ment, and humor. They want love or connection, but they need money. Equipped with mostly meager educations and varying degrees of sophistication, they bounce off one another like bumper cars, everyone’s actions affecting everyone else’s. Gainful employment

BO OKS is in short supply; vices take hold, whether ugly addic- tions or minor gambling habits; and in Under the Falls, the criminality moves beyond small-time hustles. Russo’s townsfolk do one another the courtesy, when necessary, of pretending not to see what’s in front of them; they also fight, make up, make love, and, above all, tolerate one another. We tend to think that, in hollowed-out towns such as the ones Russo writes about, those left behind are left behind in the apocalyptic sense: The chosen ones got raptured out, to better places with more work, more Starbucks, more Subarus. But Russo shows how anyplace is good enough if you’ve chosen it, or can tell yourself that you have. Class and cultural divides are sources of tension, but also of local cohesion, as Tyler discovers in Stone Mountain— and as Sully has known all his life. Just because Sully never went to college doesn’t mean he couldn’t have hacked it. North Bath is always suffering intruders, from downstate and especially from nearby Schuyler Springs— an obvious stand-in for Saratoga Springs, which has the college (Skidmore), the racetrack, the tourist season, and hence the money that Gloversville lacks. Sometimes these interlopers want to buy and rehab a house, and that’s where Sully is indispensable. He and a partner do the fixing up on fixer-uppers. They just want to be paid, with money and perhaps a modi- cum of respect. After Miles Anderson, a university professor from downstate, keeps him waiting for an hour to talk about some repairs on his new property, Sully gets huffy, leading Anderson to ask, pissily, if Sully wants the work or not. “ ‘Look, Mr. Anderson,’ Sully said, ‘I need the work. I’m just too old to jump up and down, okay? Inside, I’m all aflutter. Trust me.’ ” (The “aflutter” is a nice touch, hinting at the elevated vocabulary Sully can deploy when he wants to.) “ ‘Hmmm,’ Miles Anderson mused. ‘Well, I was also told you were insolent, though I sup- pose that’s to be expected. The gruff, frontier indepen- dence of the American blue-collar worker and all that.’ ” The only thing worse than new wealth threaten- ing to intrude is old wealth that has fled, leaving des- olation. In Empire Falls, there are perennial rumors about what might become of the old mill— is it true that investors from Boston have plans for it? The prologue to Under the Falls features a moving paean to the long-shuttered Stone Mountain Amusement Park. “Remember what amusement parks were like before they became corporate,” Russo writes, “before there were special lines for people who have more money than you do.” For Russo, amusement parks, with their rides and buffets and dining-room windows “left open to cap- ture the breeze off the lake,” were once the great lev- elers, places where, for a day, “you’re not poor; you’re The men who compound their bad luck with bad choices interest Russo the most. rich.” Stone Mountain Amusement Park offers an echo of the Ultimate Escape Fun Park, planned by Texas money men, that the town banker in Nobody’s Fool hopes to lure to North Bath. But the Texans, after flirting with North Bath, ultimately choose a more prosperous site, near Portland, Maine. It seems they were full of it all along. Russo never intimates that his bullshitters in the roadhouse are better men than the ones in the C-suite, or the ones with tenure, or the rock stars. (He is espe- cially withering, though, about the tenured bull shitters, the professoriat. His most beloved book may well be Straight Man, a campus satire in the tradition of King- sley Amis and David Lodge.) There’s good and bad everywhere, and Russo is alert to self- serving delu- sions wherever they surface. “I made a man’s mistakes,” Sully’s absentee father, “Big Jim” (obviously named for Russo’s own father), says at the end of his life. That has the ring of nobility, until we remember that his manly mistakes included beating his family, cheating on his wife, and drinking away his pay. Nor is it lost on the reader that he got away with his malign hijinks because, as a big man in a small town, he knew everyone, was enabled by everyone: cops, neighbors, co- workers. In Under the Falls, the town sheriff knows about, and indirectly profits from, Doc’s drug run- ning. He doesn’t approve, but in a small town, com- plicity is hard to avoid. Here’s what characters like Sully come to under- stand about hometowns, at least in their wiser moments, and what Tyler has to learn: Achieving escape velocity is one of those aspirations, like being “now and forevermore insulated against adversity,” that is forever out of reach. “It kind of feels like you’re on the clock,” Tyler reflects about his unexpected wealth and success. “Like any day now somebody’s going to notice there’s been a mistake, after which you’ll go back to being poor.” Which doesn’t mean you should simply stay put. Russo found Gloversville claustrophobic, as did his eccentric mother, whose mental illness— the subject of his 2012 memoir, the aptly titled Elsewhere— was surely exacerbated by being a dreamy, literate soul in a town of Babbitts. The two of them had to get out (Russo’s overattached mom followed him to college in Arizona), only to realize that the fight was never with the town but with themselves. After years of attempting to make a life elsewhere, she returned to Gloversville. So did her son, of course. He never really left. One of the best-selling nonfiction titles of 2014, Hard Choices runs to more than 600 pages, many of which consist of factoids copied and pasted from Clinton’s old speeches. It is possibly the least intro- spective book ever written. Her ghostwriters’ modus operandi was to take a bunch of platitudinous abstrac- tions from her time at the State Department (“The strategic fundamentals of our relationship—shared democratic values, economic imperatives and diplo- matic priorities—are moving us closer to an under- standing and a trust that reflects the convergence of values and interests”) and switch the tenses (“The stra- tegic fundamentals of our relationship with India— shared democratic values, economic imperatives, and diplomatic priorities— were pushing both countries’ interests into closer convergence”). Vance’s book never quite sinks to this level, but it does make me wonder why it was published, and for whose edification. Even by the standards of faith- driven airport nonfiction, Communion is not very interesting. Despite what the jacket copy suggests, the book is not “the story” of Vance’s conversion to Roman Catholicism, which had already been recounted in an essay published six years ago in the journal I edit, The Lamp. (Unaltered passages from it appear in the pres- ent volume without acknowledgment.) They exist to be announced breath- lessly, advertised, embargoed, analyzed via leaks and scooplets, discussed on podcasts—but their final end is to collect dust in the free pile outside used-book stores. Jordan ends up with the most eventful char- acter arc, ultimately tracking down perpetrators too: He wants them to pay, or at least not to disappear. B R I E F H I S T O R Y looks at power in a place of violence and examines what secrets it hides. Now James has written a book about people whose whole lives feel like secrets. And he has a thesis: Those who grow up learning that they are bad and do not deserve to exist—people who might get raped, maimed, or murdered for trying to be themselves—almost inevi- tably organize their life around attempts to disap- pear, escape, or else retreat to the margins, becoming (like Eddy) figures who observe others, themselves unseen, or (like Jordan) agents of vengeance who stick to the shadows. “There is a Jamaica underneath this Jamaica,” Jor- dan tells Eddy, whose more sheltered and luckier life means he might not know. It’s a metaphor, except when it’s not; the drag queens, trans women, and unhoused youth who live in Kingston’s gullies, below street level, have made it literal, as Eddy and Jordan, in flight from another mob later in the story, show us. James makes the gully dwellers and their fragile world a compelling side story, intent on present- ing a panorama of Kingston’s gay life, from those who occupy the economic heights (also literal hills) down to “all of them queens and freaks and fishboys and battymen” who “cannot and will not pass.” The survivors of Lady Musgrave Road flee to totally closeted respectability, “a safe place filled with disap- pointment,” where several remain for years; or else to 97

Culture & Critics opportunities off the island, or religious rebirth, or a near-invisible secluded life “at the top of a mountain.” We might see the whole novel as an attempt to create a stage, a space, where gay Jamaican men can honestly and fully appear, at least in retrospect. Like Brief History, The Disappearers offers a big, modernist assemblage of contrasting styles, perso- nas, and points of view. It, too, is a work of clas- sic realism, touring the social layers in a changing Kingston as its characters earn and lose money, rise and fall. But unlike Brief History, which includes gay characters but mostly isn’t about them, The Dis- appearers also belongs with those earlier chronicles of gay America that Jordan and Eddy name-check, especially John Rechy’s The Sexual Outlaw. And so it’s full of gay sex: ecstatic, conflicted, reluctant, a desperate secret or an open secret. James acknowledges occasions of sweet, mutual, that’s-how-it-should-be sex—but those happen largely offstage. Most of the on-page couplings instead mix, alarmingly, sex with violence. Some people seek humiliation; some want to inflict it. Some get hurt by their tricks. James manages not to kink-shame any- one, but he’s less interested in kink education than in displaying a sexual world where every hookup comes with scary risks: assault and battery, for example, or public exposure, or HIV in the age before retrovirals. Living in fear of “the AIDS” entails its own “long set of disappearing acts”—not just sickness and death, but shame and denial and an inability to mourn. Those risks do not keep most of James’s survi- vors from pursuing, or becoming, hookups and rent boys and hate-fucks, with and without proper lube and enemas, which the novel—appropriately, even necessarily— describes: Responsible writing about anal sex has to mention those things, and James does. He wants to bring his gay men’s sex lives into the light. The men, however, keep trying to “erase themselves,” learning how to “make yourself into the kind of person nobody wants to see.” Early on, Eddy claims, “I don’t think about it a lot,” and yet he’s never unaware of being “part of an us that people just want to beat to death.” Or bury alive. THE DISAPPEARERS M a r l o n Ja m e s RIVERHEAD T h e n o v e l opens up many pleasures for literary readers, in its pacing, in its observations, and especially in the ventriloquism of Havelock’s old-school prose (he even writes one letter in the obsolescent gay slang Polari). But it’s not, mostly, a book about pleasure: These lives are often—realistically—scary or sad. We should not label them tragedies, though, because that implies a controlling divinity, or at least a fixed fate. As Havelock insists, “We need to stop calling atrocities tragic.” The Disappearers is, among other things, one novel responding to many atrocities. 98 SEPTEMBER 2026 When you grow up surrounded by people who hate you for what you are and whom you love, it’s tough to disentangle their hate from self-hate, and either one from a wish to die. And it’s not just the cast from Lady Musgrave Road that conflates self-destruction with self-fashioning, death with destiny. So does the music of Kurt Cobain, the most important among the cultural touchstones that give Jordan and Eddy alternatives to Kings- ton. They listen to Nirvana, and to the rock bands that Cobain recommended—“music that people who hate me don’t like,” Jordan says—more than to “Peter Metro and Admiral Bailey” and other hit- makers from the island. Major characters also find allies in older gay novels, like Rechy’s, and in comic books. “Come to think of it, my life is exactly like X-Men. I served a world, in this case the world of cool boys,” Eddy decides early on, “only to have those same boys abuse and brutalize me.” The heroic mutants of Marvel Comics— Nightcrawler, who looks like a devil; Storm, whom one gully queen resembles; and the rest—promise one way to survive the Kingston expe- rience, even though, in the particular issue of X-Men that Eddy covets, the X-Men literally disappear. Renaissance writings—Shakespeare’s sonnets and King Lear, Christopher Marlowe’s Edward II—give James additional scaffolding for his stories about attachment and found family, literal torture and tortured love. The strongest subplot links the fate of Eddy’s half-Chinese crush back to the sonnets, as well as to Herbert’s play. The weakest subplot turns Jordan into an obsessive, predictable avenger, less like one of the X-Men than like a Jamaican Joker, with a twist that’s no twist at all if you’ve seen horror films. Yet up to that obvious final act, the Eddy-and- Jordan pairing works elegantly, showing two sides of the same damaged face. Still, any reader will feel for Jordan when he exclaims, late in the novel, “My ghost suffering makes me want to scream.” He means both that, compared with people dying of AIDS, he isn’t genu- inely suffering (though he is), and that he feels like a disembodied outcast, a kind of ghost. The Disap- pearers ends up as a violence-driven protest, a scream of rage—like Nirvana’s final album—against a world that keeps trying to kill people like him and then pretends that they asked for it, or that they never existed. The novel is a superbly fashioned instrument for showing what felt wrong, what went wrong, in Jamaica in the late 1980s and ’90s, and what’s still wrong in other places, too, where people who grow up marginalized get blamed for their own persecu- tion, or else celebrated as brave exceptions when, against the odds, they succeed.

BO OKS The fantastic unfairness—especially if it’s as brutal and direct as what James depicts—might make you a vanisher or an avenger (like Jordan). Or it might instead make you a chronicler (like Eddy and Petra), a maker of memorials, even a rescuer for people who want to be rescued—people who get sick of trying to disappear. And some do: Most of the survivors from Lady Musgrave Road, however wounded, find a way to forge on. Some (like Havelock) even keep trying at “building something—I don’t know, a safe place, a room of one’s own and world so you can let your hair down so to speak?” In James’s wildly patriarchal Jamaica, the struggle to live as a gay man means a struggle to become and remain some kind of man, whatever you like to do in bed. Life is, or seems to be, all about men: Women appear in the book but never narrate (as one does in Brief History), and barely say how they feel. That’s part of the point of The Disappearers, in which the same men who persecute gay desire want women to disappear. As in any binary opposition, men learn to define themselves against their supposed other: “Nothing more shameful for a man than to be treated like a woman,” one character thinks, an idea all too familiar in the contemporary United States as well. Among the seven people who survive the Lady Musgrave Road assault, James traces some future for all but one: outside or inside Jamaica, in sham marriages that fail or desk jobs that allow them to subsist, and even in fragile, comforting, long-delayed reunions. As for that one actor who just drops out of the plot, maybe he died. After all, his “own family prefer him gone.” Or maybe that person was never a man in the first place and built a solid life else- where as an adult woman, her boyhood deleted for good—what trans people in earlier generations called “woodworking” (fading into the woodwork). Within The Disappearers, that’s one character’s speculation, dismissed as soon as it’s raised. But it’s also another hint of hope. And this novel, which ends in 2005, does offer hope: not just for gay Jamai- can men but for trans teens, non binary adults, and anyone else since then who’s felt as though their society has kept asking them to hide, or lie, or die, or just go away. The Disappearers is a harrowing book, to be sure, but never nihilist, or defeatist, or cynical. Its joy in ultimate survival comes through. Musicians frequently encounter both of these extreme views of music’s most mys- terious profession. It’s not surprising that conductors elicit sus- picion as well as adu- lation. The very act of conducting— waving a wand to summon ravishing or ethereal or earsplitting sounds— can look like either SEPTEMBER 2026
